description: Hacettepe University Computer Engineering and Artificial Intelligence Engineering based participants.
summary:
AKBUGA (Autonomous Knowledge-based Biomedical Unit for Guidance & Analysis) is a crew health box for long-duration missions. On a long mission “normal” itself drifts: core temperature rises about 1 °C over 2.5 months, diastolic pressure falls, sleep settles near six hours. Fixed population thresholds turn that drift into a stream of false alarms, and a crew that is told “you are ill” ten times a day stops listening.

AKBUGA judges each crewmember against their own drifting in-flight baseline. A deviation reaches the crew only after it passes six false-alarm gates: personal baseline, persistence, a related second signal, context, re-measurement and tier. The environmental limits come from NASA-STD-3001, so a high cabin CO₂ level is flagged as an environment finding, not as an illness. When an emergency is real, AKBUGA announces it to the crew and guides them hands-free, by voice, through written, sourced instructions, including microgravity CPR.

On a synthetic 180-day, four-crew mission, fixed thresholds raise 8.4 false alarms per crewmember per day; AKBUGA raises 0.04 and misses none of the three planted events. This matters because, far from Earth, an alarm the crew ignores is as dangerous as no alarm at all.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

AKBUGA is a crew health box for long-duration missions. It brings four input groups (a garment with ECG, a camera and microphone, measurement devices and cabin sensors) into one place. Every crewmember is judged against their own drifting in-flight baseline, not against population limits.

An emergency can start in three ways:

1. Manual SOS: a crewmember presses the button or says "SOS".

2. Rule-based SOS: one of the only two signals allowed to alarm on its own fires, SpO₂ or a malignant ECG rhythm.

3. Classifier SOS: a classifier scores ten problem classes derived from NASA's medical condition list, and its rulebook confirms the class with class-specific tests.

Every automatic deviation must pass six false-alarm gates before anyone is interrupted: personal baseline, persistence, a related second signal, context (exercise, sleep, EVA, circadian alignment), re-measurement and tier. Only an SOS interrupts by voice; slow trends become a silent "attention" notice. An environmental gate built on NASA-STD-3001 limits flags the cabin instead of the person, so a headache during high CO₂ is not escalated to an emergency.

When an emergency is real, AKBUGA announces who and where to the whole crew. It reads back what it heard and asks closed-ended verification questions. It orders a measurement only when the result can change the next step, and reads the instruction steps word for word from a written, sourced instruction set covering all eleven classes, including microgravity CPR. The crew can answer while AKBUGA is still speaking, and an echo filter removes the system's own voice from what the microphone hears. Every reading and answer is streamed to the flight surgeon on Earth over a simulated light delay; a patient who can be held stable waits for Earth's instructions after first aid. A five-minute morning check feeds every daily value, and a 3D body view shows which region needs attention and why.

What benefits does it have?

- Alarms the crew can trust. On a synthetic 180-day, four-crew mission, fixed thresholds raise 8.4 false alarms per crewmember per day; AKBUGA raises 0.04 and misses none of the three planted events.

- Hands-free guidance by voice that a non-physician crewmember can follow.

- Traceability. Every threshold and every instruction step carries its source, or is openly marked as an assumption.

- It still works without connectivity. An offline decision tree drives the flow when no language model is available.

What is the intended impact?

As missions go further from Earth, communication delays grow to minutes and the crew becomes its own first responder. Our goal is a medical assistant that stays quiet when nothing is wrong and acts immediately when something is. A system that cries wolf ten times a day is ignored on the day it matters. The architecture is meant to carry over to remote settings on Earth as well, such as polar stations and submarines.

What tools did we use?

- Languages and frameworks: TypeScript, React, Vite; Vitest for 238 automated tests.

- 3D body view: three.js, with the CC0 MakeHuman base mesh.

- Voice: the browser's Web Speech API for speech recognition and speech synthesis.

- Language model : a provider-neutral connection, configurable for Claude, OpenAI, Gemini or a local Ollama model. Only the local Ollama path has been run live.

- Hardware: no physical hardware. Sensors are simulated with a synthetic mission generator in which drifts follow published spaceflight magnitudes.

- Hosting: the published site is a static build on GitHub Pages and runs the offline decision tree.

How is the project creative?

- The drifting baseline itself is the reference. Physiology that shifts in space is treated as the new normal, not as illness.

- The language model never writes instructions; it only chooses. It selects a class, a question, a measurement or a step through tool calls, following the sequential-diagnosis pattern of Microsoft's MAI-DxO. A rule executor refuses unsafe choices.

- Urgency decides how long the system waits for the model. In time-critical moments the offline tree acts at once and the model's late answer is used only if it still fits.

- The environment is a gate, not a background value: NASA requirements decide whether a finding belongs to the cabin or to the person.

What factors did the team consider?

- Scientific honesty. The false-alarm numbers and the classifier accuracy come from synthetic data and are not clinical evidence. The personal thresholds are our assumptions, because no validated spaceflight reference exists. The instruction set was drafted with SI from cited sources and has not had a medical review.

- Licensing. Copyrighted resuscitation guidelines are cited, not copied; microgravity CPR is adapted from an open-access (CC BY 4.0) guideline with attribution.

- Safety. Ultrasound images are never interpreted, cardiac arrest is never held for Earth, and an unclear answer is asked again, never guessed.

- Usability. Hands-free operation, spoken read-back, and buttons and text as a fallback when voice fails.
